notes.summary: Profit, loss and discount is about cost price, selling price and marked price, and it is one of the most asked arithmetic topics. SSC asks 1 to 3 questions in Tier 1 and 2 to 3 in Tier 2, mostly on marked price and discount, successive discounts and dishonest dealers. Nearly every question is solved by writing each step as a multiplier.

concepts.title: The basic words
concepts.body:
• Cost price (CP): what the seller paid. Any extra spend on repairs, transport or tax that the seller pays is added to the CP.
  • Selling price (SP): what the buyer pays.
  • Profit = SP − CP when SP is more. Loss = CP − SP when SP is less.
  • Profit% and loss% are always on the CP unless the question says otherwise: Profit% = Profit/CP × 100.

Example: bought for ₹400, sold for ₹460. Profit = 60, profit% = 60/400 × 100 = 15%.

Example: a scooter is bought for ₹4,700 and ₹800 is spent on repairs. It is sold for ₹5,800. CP = 5,500, profit = 300, profit% = 300/5,500 × 100 = 5 5/11%.

concepts.title: Finding SP or CP with multipliers
concepts.body:
• SP = CP × (100 + profit%)/100, or CP × (100 − loss%)/100.
  • CP = SP × 100/(100 + profit%), or SP × 100/(100 − loss%).

Example: sold for ₹720 at a 10% loss. CP = 720 × 100/90 = ₹800. To gain 15%, SP = 800 × 1.15 = ₹920.

Short cut: you can go straight from one SP to another. New SP = old SP × (100 + new profit%)/(100 + old profit%). Here 720 × 115/90 = 920.

concepts.title: The ratio method for CP and SP
concepts.body:
Turn the percent into a fraction and read CP : SP directly.

Profit or lossFractionCP : SP
10% profit1/1010 : 11
12.5% profit1/88 : 9
20% profit1/55 : 6
25% profit1/44 : 5
33 1/3% profit1/33 : 4
16 2/3% loss1/66 : 5
20% loss1/55 : 4
25% loss1/44 : 3

Example: 25% profit and SP = ₹500. CP : SP = 4 : 5, so 5 parts = 500, one part = 100, CP = ₹400.

concepts.title: Marked price and discount
concepts.body:
• Marked price (MP) or list price is the price printed on the item.
  • Discount is always on the MP: SP = MP × (100 − discount%)/100.
  • Markup% = (MP − CP)/CP × 100.

Example: MP ₹800 with 15% discount. SP = 800 × 0.85 = ₹680.

Example: a customer paid ₹330 after a 45% discount. MP = 330 × 100/55 = ₹600.

concepts.title: The MP to CP ratio (fastest method)
concepts.body:
Because CP × (100 + profit%) = MP × (100 − discount%), we get

MP/CP = (100 + profit%)/(100 − discount%)

Example: discount 10% and profit 26%. MP/CP = 126/90 = 1.4, so MP is 40% above CP.

Example: goods marked 42% above CP and sold at 15% discount. SP/CP = 1.42 × 0.85 = 1.207, so profit is 20.7%.

Useful pair: marking up by x% and then giving x% discount always gives a loss of x²/100%.

concepts.title: Successive discounts
concepts.body:
Discounts of a% and b% one after another equal a single discount of a + b − ab/100%.

  • 20% and 10%: 20 + 10 − 2 = 28%.
  • Three discounts: multiply the multipliers. 10%, 20%, 25% gives 0.9 × 0.8 × 0.75 = 0.54, a single discount of 46%.
  • Order does not matter.

Two successive discounts always give less than their simple sum. Discounts of 20% and 10% give 28%, so a single 30% discount is better for the buyer.

concepts.title: Overall profit percent on combined deals
concepts.body:
When there are several deals, add all the CPs and all the SPs, then find the profit% on the total CP. Do not add or average the percents unless the CPs are equal.

Example: a machine bought for ₹5,000 and sold for ₹6,000; another bought for ₹8,000 and sold for ₹10,000. Total CP 13,000, total SP 16,000, profit 3,000, profit% = 3,000/13,000 × 100 = 23 1/13%.

If the CPs are equal, the overall profit% is the simple average of the two percents.

concepts.title: Two articles at the same selling price
concepts.body:
• Same SP, gain x% on one and loss x% on the other: there is always a loss of x²/100%.
  • Different percents: find each CP from the SP, add, then compare with total SP.

Example: two items sold at ₹990 each, one at 10% gain, one at 10% loss. Loss = 10²/100 = 1%.

Same CP for both: the overall percent is the simple average. With different CPs, it is a weighted average (use alligation).

concepts.title: Dishonest dealer and false weights
concepts.body:
If a seller sells at cost price but gives a smaller weight, he gains on the missing part.

Gain% = (true weight − false weight)/false weight × 100.

  • 900 g for 1 kg: gain = 100/900 × 100 = 11 1/9%.
  • With a markup or discount too: SP/CP multiplier = (price multiplier) × (true weight/false weight). Example: sells at 10% above CP and uses 800 g for 1 kg. Multiplier = 1.1 × 1000/800 = 1.375, gain 37.5%.
  • Cheating while buying too (takes 1,100 g as 1 kg): multiply by 1,100/1,000 as well.

concepts.title: Articles and rates
concepts.body:
• If the SP of x articles = the CP of y articles, then profit% = (y − x)/x × 100. A negative answer means loss.
  • Rates like "a for ₹b": make the number of articles equal by taking the LCM, then compare money.

Example: SP of 40 = CP of 50. Profit% = 10/40 × 100 = 25%.

Example: bought at 10 for ₹15 and sold at 16 for ₹40. CP of one = 1.5, SP of one = 2.5. Profit% = 1/1.5 × 100 = 66 2/3%.

concepts.title: Buy some, get some free
concepts.body:
"Buy x, get y free" means the customer pays for x but gets x + y. Effective discount% = y/(x + y) × 100.

Example: buy 3 get 1 free. Discount = 1/4 × 100 = 25%.

When this is combined with another discount, treat it as one more successive discount.

concepts.title: Chain of sale
concepts.body:
When an item passes through several hands, multiply all the multipliers.

Final price = first CP × (1 + p₁/100)(1 + p₂/100)… Use (1 − l/100) for a loss.

Example: A sells to B at 20% profit and B sells to C at 25% profit. C pays ₹600. A’s CP = 600 ÷ (1.2 × 1.25) = 600/1.5 = ₹400.

concepts.title: Part sold at profit, rest at loss
concepts.body:
Find the overall profit as a weighted average of the parts. Take the total CP as 100.

Example: half the goods sold at 20% profit and half at 10% loss. Overall = (20 − 10)/2 = 5% profit.

Example: 1/3 at 15% profit, 1/4 at 20% profit and the rest at 20% loss. Overall = 15/3 + 20/4 − 20 × 5/12 = 5 + 5 − 8 1/3 = 1 2/3% profit.

concepts.title: Profit on selling price
concepts.body:
Some questions give the profit or loss as a percent of SP. Convert it:

  • Profit p% on SP = p/(100 − p) × 100% on CP.
  • Profit P% on CP = P/(100 + P) × 100% on SP.
  • Loss l% on SP = l/(100 + l) × 100% on CP.

Example: 20% profit on SP. Take SP = 100, profit = 20, CP = 80. Profit on CP = 20/80 = 25%.

concepts.title: When CP or SP changes
concepts.body:
A change in rupees matches a change in percent of the CP.

  • Sold at 10% loss; had it been sold for ₹60 more, gain would be 5%. The extra ₹60 = 15% of CP, so CP = ₹400.
  • If both CP and SP change, write the new CP and new SP in terms of the old CP and form one equation.
  • Profit at SP₁ equals loss at SP₂: CP = (SP₁ + SP₂)/2.

varieties.name: Cost price, selling price and profit percent
varieties.how: Find CP and SP for the same quantity, then profit% = (SP − CP)/CP × 100. Use multipliers to go between CP and SP.

example.q: A man buys 10 identical articles for ₹15 and sells each for ₹1.70. What is his profit percentage?

varieties.name: Change in selling or cost price
varieties.how: The extra rupees equal the gap between the two percents, taken on CP. Find CP, then the asked price.

example.q: A person sold an article at a loss of 15%. Had he sold it for ₹30.60 more, he would have gained 9%. At what price should he sell it to gain 10%?

varieties.name: Marked price and discount
varieties.how: Use SP = MP × (100 − d)/100 and MP/CP = (100 + profit%)/(100 − discount%).

example.q: A merchant marks his goods 42% above cost price and sells them at a 15% discount. What is his profit percent, to the nearest integer?

varieties.name: Successive discounts
varieties.how: Multiply the multipliers: MP × (1 − a/100)(1 − b/100) = SP. Or use a + b − ab/100 for the single discount.

example.q: An article with marked price ₹480 is sold for ₹288 after successive discounts of 25% and x%. Find x.

varieties.name: Dishonest dealer and false weights
varieties.how: Gain% = (true − false)/false × 100. To find the false weight, false = true × 100/(100 + gain%).

example.q: A dishonest trader says he sells at cost price but uses a false weight and gains 12.5%. What weight does he use for 1 kg?

varieties.name: Cost of x articles equals price of y articles
varieties.how: SP of x = CP of y gives profit% = (y − x)/x × 100. For rates, find the price of one article each way.

example.q: If the selling price of 40 articles is equal to the cost price of 50 articles, what is the profit or loss percent?
steps: Positive, so it is a profit

varieties.name: Part sold at profit, rest at loss
varieties.how: Take total CP as 100 (or one unit), find the money from each part, add, and compare with the total CP.

example.q: A trader marks his goods 40% above cost. He sells 70% of the goods at the marked price and the rest at a 40% discount on the marked price. Find his profit percent.

varieties.name: Two articles at the same price
varieties.how: Same SP with x% gain and x% loss: loss of x²/100%. Otherwise find each CP from the SP and compare totals.

example.q: Two articles are sold for ₹9,720 each. On one the seller gains 8% and on the other he loses 10%. What is his overall gain or loss?

varieties.name: Chain of sale
varieties.how: Multiply the multipliers of every step. Divide the final price by this product to get the first cost.

example.q: A manufacturer sells a gas stove to a shopkeeper at 10% profit, and the shopkeeper sells it to a customer at 15% profit. The customer pays ₹2,530. What did it cost the manufacturer?

varieties.name: Buy some, get some free
varieties.how: Buy x, get y free: discount% = y/(x + y) × 100.

example.q: A shop offers "buy 5 water bottles, get 1 free". What is the effective discount percent?

varieties.name: Profit or loss on selling price
varieties.how: Take SP = 100. Find profit or loss in rupees from SP, get CP, then work on CP as usual.

example.q: On selling an article for ₹800, a person loses 20% of the selling price. At what price should he sell it to gain 25% on the cost price?

tips: Profit and loss percents are on CP. Discount is on MP. Keep the base straight.
Use MP/CP = (100 + profit%)/(100 − discount%) for any question with both a discount and a profit.
Write every change as a multiplier (× 1.2, × 0.85) and multiply. Chains, successive discounts and false weights all become one line.
Learn CP : SP pairs: 20% profit is 5 : 6, 25% profit is 4 : 5, 12.5% profit is 8 : 9.
For the same SP with x% gain and x% loss, the answer is always a loss of x²/100%, so you do not need the SP.
Take CP = 100 when no amount is given.
traps: Two discounts of 20% and 10% are not 30%. The single discount is 28%.
Repair and transport costs paid by the seller are part of the CP.
Overall profit% on two deals is not the average of the two percents unless the CPs are equal.
A loss given "on the selling price" must be converted to CP before using normal formulas.
In false-weight questions, divide by the false weight, not by 1,000 g.
